newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Soldiers warned after rampage in Zaire town.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers warned after rampage in Zaire town.

text.p: The army commander in the Zairean town of Kisangani told soldiers there on Sunday that they would be shot if they carried weapons in the streets after two nights of shooting and looting.
The commanding general issued the warning over local radio after drunk or ill-disciplined soldiers who arrived after defeat by Tutsi rebels in east Zaire ran amok in parts of the town.

Earlier, Roman Catholic Church workers and local businessmen keen to help displaced Zaireans and refugees fleeing the Tutsi revolt in the east said a charter flight over the region had found no evidence of a major exodus.

"There's no problem. Although shots were heard there is no systematic looting in the town," regional governor Lombeya Bosongo told Reuters, adding that troops had already started to return to the battle front.
"Already this morning there was a movement in the opposite direction. The men are going back," he said.
Kisangani Chamber of Commerce and church workers are trying to locate and help the refugees and displaced Zaireans.

"A pilot who flew over Lubutu and Walikale this morning saw a few groups on the road. That was all," one missionary said. "It may be that they are taking forest paths but we may be talking of only a few thousands instead of many thousands."
Raymond Mokeni, chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, said that if the refugees could be supplied where they were there would be no need for them to come all the way to Kisangani.

"We are organising a convoy to bring back the sick and supply what we can on the ground. Because of the insecurity along the road both the displaced and local villagers spend the day in the forest and only return to the road at night."

Kisangani is the last outpost of tenuous Zairean authority before tens of thousands of square kilometres (miles) of forest and hills in which an unknown number of Hutu refugees from Rwanda or Burundi and displaced Zaireans are hiding.
Heavy overnight gunfire rocked the town on Friday night and at least three businesses were looted. "The tension here is too much. I will have to get my family out," one businessman said.
Soldiers cruise the usually quiet streets in vehicles commandeered from aid workers before the retreat.
Calm returned on Saturday and shops reopened, but fresh shooting and looting took place on Saturday night.
An unconfirmed report said one soldier had been shot dead on Friday night by troops seeking to restore order. There were no other immediate reports of casualties.

Kisangani, about 500 km (325 miles) from the conflict zone, is a likely staging post for any relief operation for Hutu refugees who are believed to have trekked west to escape the fighting and the danger of reprisals from rival Tutsis.
Foreign aid workers left eastern Zaire over a week ago as insecurity spread to the huge refugee camps of Goma and Bukavu.

The whereabouts of many of the 1.2 million Hutus from the camps remains a mystery but reports filtering out of eastern Zaire talk of refugees dying from thirst and exhaustion in the granite hills. Aid groups fear cholera and dysentery epidemics.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of Tutsis. Zaire says Tutsi-led Rwanda is behind the revolt in the east.

Meanwhile, 11 tonnes of aid from Spain -- food, blankets and tents -- arrived in the Zairean capital Kinshasa on Sunday. Officials said it would be given to the national Red Cross for distribution to displaced Zaireans, possibly via Kisangani.
